note: Two independent drafts of the same case, written without knowledge of each other in round 46 batches 2 and 3. They disagree on the death count (4 vs 3), on confidence (documented vs contested) and on which sources were opened. Produce ONE reconciled case.

draft_from_batch_2.title: Bandayi and Mege: houses demolished beside the Kibali gold mine
draft_from_batch_2.place: Bandayi and Mege, Durba, Haut-Uele, Democratic Republic of the Congo
draft_from_batch_2.point: Durba town in Haut-Uele; Bandayi and Mege are the adjoining neighbourhoods next to the Kibali gold mine.

lenders.name: Barrick Gold Corporation
lenders.role: Holds 45% of the Kibali joint venture and operates the mine; it acquired the interest through its 2019 merger with Randgold (Canada's National Contact Point, 2024).

lenders.name: AngloGold Ashanti plc
lenders.role: Holds 45% of Kibali. The UK contact point said that share gave it significant leverage over the mine and its operating partners (OECD Watch).

lenders.name: SOKIMO
lenders.role: Congolese state mining company, holder of the remaining 10% of Kibali (Canada's National Contact Point, 2024; Reuters, 2021).

draft_from_batch_2.conditions: The provincial government cleared the ground. Officials called the buildings unauthorised structures that obstructed the activities of Kibali Gold Mines SA; the governor of Haut-Uele authorised the operation and the provincial mines minister supervised it, with the army and the national police carrying it out (Avocats Sans Frontieres, 2022). The governor's office said the occupation of the two villages violated Kibali's rights (Reuters). No loan condition was found.

companies.name: Barrick Gold Corporation
companies.role: 45% owner and operator of the Kibali mine
companies.desc: Canadian gold mining company. Canada's contact point records that it holds 45% of the Kibali joint venture and operates the mine, an interest obtained in the 2019 Randgold merger.

companies.name: AngloGold Ashanti plc
companies.role: 45% owner of the Kibali mine; respondent to the 2024 complaint at the UK contact point
companies.desc: Gold miner incorporated in England and Wales with its headquarters in Denver and a large corporate office in Johannesburg; it moved its primary share listing to the New York Stock Exchange on 25 September 2023 (company release).

companies.name: Kibali Goldmines SA
companies.role: The mine company whose activities the demolitions were said to clear
companies.desc: Joint venture company holding the Kibali mine, which produced 364,000 ounces of gold in 2020 (Reuters).

draft_from_batch_2.community: PAX reports about 2,500 homes demolished in October 2021 in Mege and Bandayi, two densely built neighbourhoods next to Durba. Avocats Sans Frontieres counts 953 structures destroyed on 19 and 20 October 2021 - 947 houses, one school, two shops and three churches - and says 610 of those affected were still without shelter or basic services a year later. People had been resettled out of the two villages earlier and later moved back in (Reuters). More than 2,360 households signed the February 2024 complaint, which asks for money to support the families and help them relocate (OECD Watch).
draft_from_batch_2.suppression: Security forces put down a solidarity protest in Durba on 21 and 22 October 2021. Avocats Sans Frontieres reports at least four people killed and more than fifteen injured, and records arbitrary arrests, intimidation and attempted abductions of community leaders who pressed the victims' claims. Reuters, citing the governor's office, reported that shots were fired and at least one death and several wounded were confirmed.
draft_from_batch_2.killed_note: Avocats Sans Frontieres reports at least four people killed when the Congolese army and national police suppressed the Durba protest against the demolitions on 21 and 22 October 2021. Reuters, citing the governor's office, confirmed at least one death and several wounded and did not say who fired. The forces were acting on the provincial governor's authorisation to clear ground described as obstructing the mine. Kibali said the demonstration did not take place on its concession and was not connected to the company, and Barrick denied directing or controlling local police.
draft_from_batch_2.outcome: The complainants first took the case to Canada's contact point against Barrick on 10 May 2022. That contact point shared its initial assessment in August 2023 and offered its good offices only on the allegation that the company contributed to human rights harm from the 2021 exclusion-zone resettlement, not on the Durba police response or the tax claims, and stressed this was not a finding on whether the Guidelines had been observed. After one dialogue on 1 December 2023 it judged further mediation unlikely to resolve the matter, approved its final statement on 19 April 2024 with recommendations and a follow-up six months later, and took no position on the claims; Barrick denied directing or controlling local police. A linked complaint to the UK contact point in 2022 was withdrawn. The UK contact point accepted the February 2024 complaint against AngloGold Ashanti on 12 December 2025, offered mediation to both parties and said a further examination was needed to establish whether due diligence had been applied consistently with the Guidelines over the October 2021 incidents (OECD Watch). The governor's office suspended the evictions after the protest and opened an inquiry (Reuters), and the justice minister told judicial authorities to investigate and prosecute where warranted; Avocats Sans Frontieres was still urging those investigations forward a year later and asking Kibali Gold Mines SA to compensate and help resettle the victims.

draft_from_batch_2.confidence_note: The demolitions and the killings are reported outside the complaint, and the counts do not agree. PAX puts about 2,500 homes demolished in October 2021; Avocats Sans Frontieres counts 953 structures on 19-20 October and at least four killed and more than fifteen injured in the Durba protest; Reuters, citing the governor's office, reported at least one killed and several wounded. PAX reports no deaths. Who is answerable is disputed: the army and police carried out the demolitions on the provincial governor's authorisation, Kibali said the demonstration was not on its concession and was not connected to the company and described the operation as the provincial government evicting illegal settlers from a government-defined exclusion zone, and Barrick denied directing or controlling local police. Canada's contact point took no position on the claims and the UK contact point has reached no finding.

draft_from_batch_2.whole: Kibali produced 364,000 ounces of gold in 2020, the year before the demolitions (Reuters). A year after them, Avocats Sans Frontieres reported 610 people still without shelter or basic services and asked Kibali Gold Mines SA to pay compensation and help with resettlement. No figure was found for compensation paid. More than 2,360 households from the two neighbourhoods signed the 2024 complaint; Canada's contact point declined to take up their tax claims, and its 2024 process ended after a single dialogue meeting.

draft_from_batch_3.title: Kibali Gold Mine: the Bandayi and Mege demolitions
draft_from_batch_3.place: Durba, Haut-Uélé, Democratic Republic of the Congo
draft_from_batch_3.point: Durba town in Watsa territory. The Bandayi and Mege neighbourhoods next to it sat inside the Kibali mine's Exclusion Zone B; the mine itself is about 3 km to the south.

lenders.name: Barrick Gold Corporation (Canada), 45% owner and operator of Kibali Goldmines SA (foreign owner)
lenders.role: Operates the mine for the joint venture. PAX says Kibali and Barrick lobbied the provincial authorities repeatedly over the people living in Exclusion Zone B and played a substantial role in the demolitions, and that Barrick's chief executive visited the mine less than ten days before they began.

lenders.name: AngloGold Ashanti PLC, 45% owner (foreign owner)
lenders.role: Holds 45% of Kibali Goldmines SA. It told the UK NCP that Barrick operates the mine and that it does not manage day-to-day operations; the UK NCP found its 45% stake gives it significant leverage over the mine and its partners.

lenders.name: Société Minière de Kilo-Moto (SOKIMO), 10% owner
lenders.role: DRC state-owned mining company, the third shareholder in the joint venture.

draft_from_batch_3.conditions: No loan or aid conditions were found; the outside money here is the two owners' own equity. What the demolitions followed instead was an administrative step: PAX records a joint Kibali-provincial government workshop in January 2021 that recommended demolishing structures in the exclusion zone, and the provincial governor's creation of a Special Demolition Commission in March 2021.

companies.name: Barrick Gold Corporation
companies.desc: Canadian gold mining company. PAX names it as the operator of Kibali, which it calls Africa's largest gold mine.

companies.name: AngloGold Ashanti PLC
companies.hq: Johannesburg, South Africa at the time of the demolitions
companies.desc: Gold miner formed in April 2004 from the merger of AngloGold and Ashanti Goldfields Corporation (ActionAid). The UK NCP records that it completed a corporate restructuring giving it a UK domicile on 25 September 2023.

draft_from_batch_3.community: PAX records demolitions in Bandayi on 17, 18 and part of 19 October 2021 and in Mege on 20 and 21 October 2021. More than 2,500 houses were pulled down with heavy machinery by Congolese authorities, including the Special Demolition Commission, police and military. A parliamentary mission counted 1,550 houses plus a nursery, a primary school and a secondary school in Bandayi, and 956 houses in Mege; lawmakers also recorded the demolition of a church and a school and the unemployment that followed. PAX estimates about 2,500 households were left homeless, among them children, pregnant women and older people, and says security forces arbitrarily arrested and mistreated people from Mege and Bandayi, some held for several months. More than 2,360 households signed the complaints.
draft_from_batch_3.suppression: Protests in Durba on 22 October 2021 were met with live ammunition from state security forces. A parliamentary mission found four people shot dead, including one soldier, and 14 wounded, and described a disproportionate use of force; at least one police station was destroyed. PAX also documents arbitrary arrests and mistreatment of residents, with some detentions lasting several months.
draft_from_batch_3.killed_note: At least three protesters were shot dead by Congolese state security forces during the 22 October 2021 protests in Durba against the demolitions, according to media, civil society and lawmakers as collected by PAX. The parliamentary mission's count of four dead includes a soldier whom protesters killed, so three is the number attributable to the security forces. The demolitions were carried out by a provincial Special Demolition Commission with police and military; Kibali denies any involvement in the violence.
draft_from_batch_3.outcome: Community members filed with the UK NCP in 2022 against AngloGold Ashanti and withdrew in July 2022 because the company was not then incorporated in the UK. The Canadian NCP accepted the Barrick complaint and offered mediation on one allegation only, that the company contributed to adverse human rights impacts from the resettlement; it did not publish its initial assessment and treated the other issues, including tax, as not material or not sufficiently substantiated. It facilitated a dialogue in December 2023, concluded further engagement was unlikely to resolve the issue, and recommended that Barrick disclose more about its dealings with government authorities and local police over the 2021 events and keep engaging with the community. A fresh complaint against AngloGold Ashanti, now UK-domiciled, was received by the UK NCP on 22 November 2024; on 12 December 2025 the UK NCP accepted six paragraphs for further examination, rejecting the tax allegations as unsubstantiated, and said expressly that this does not mean it has concluded the Guidelines were breached. On 27 July 2026 the same households filed against AngloGold Ashanti at the US NCP.
draft_from_batch_3.whole: Kibali was commissioned in September 2013 after about $1.7 billion of development and produced 814,000 ounces of gold in 2019, above the 600,000 ounces a year projected for its first twelve years (Wikipedia). PAX calls it Africa's largest gold mine, with permits covering 1,836 square kilometres, supplying about 60% of Haut-Uélé provincial government revenue, projected to run to 2040, and paying US$200 million in dividends to shareholders in 2021. The resettlement figures are the company's own and are disputed: Barrick said in 2022 that over 20,000 individuals from at least 4,000 households had been moved, and in November 2024 that 16,277 project-affected people in 3,777 households had been resettled between 2010 and 2013; PAX counts more than 36,000 people relocated across three campaigns and rejects Barrick's account of Mege and Bandayi. PAX found one EITI-reported payment of US$58,501 in 2015 labelled 'indemnisation Mege'.

draft_from_batch_3.confidence_note: The demolitions, the schools lost and the shooting deaths are recorded by a parliamentary mission reported by Reuters and by PAX's field research, outside the complaints. Barrick disputes PAX's account: it says the residents of Mege and Bandayi were 'illegal occupants' of Exclusion Zone B who had all been resettled in September 2013, that only 26 isolated households remained in the zone, that the October 2021 uprising was not linked to the government-led resettlement, and that Kibali had no involvement; it called PAX's initial findings inaccurate. Kibali's country director said residents ignored concrete boundary beacons and that the government did not act on the company's requests to restore them. The death toll differs between sources: the parliamentary mission counted four dead including a soldier killed by protesters; PAX's text gives at least three in one place and at least four in another. The UK NCP has made no finding on the facts, and the Canadian NCP published no initial assessment.
